title: Pseudo-relativistic fermions and topological states in zinc-blende semiconductors and their heterostructures (Habilitation thesis)
abstract: Tracing my scientific path from many-body physics in semiconductor nanostructures to topological quantum matter, this Habilitation à diriger des recherches (HDR) memoir presents only part of my research since defending two PhD theses in Toulouse and Nizhny Novgorod in 2011. Focusing on pseudo-relativistic fermions and topological states in zinc-blende semiconductors and their heterostructures, it highlights my independent research program: identifying physical problems, developing predictive theories, and initiating new directions with experimentalists.   The first part addresses Kane fermions in bulk HgCdTe: temperature-driven band inversion, domain-wall states, the collapse of Landau levels in crossed electric and magnetic fields, and disorder-induced topological transitions. The second examines pressure-, temperature-, and disorder-driven phase transitions in single and double HgTe quantum wells (QWs), including bilayer-graphene-like semimetals and a two-dimensional higher-order topological insulator (2D HOTI) phase beyond the minimal BHZ model. The third develops three-layer InAs/Ga(In)Sb QWs as a III-V platform for massless Dirac fermions, large-gap quantum spin Hall insulators, 2D HOTI phases, and semimetals with quadratic band touching, and discusses InAs$_{x}$Sb$_{1-x}$/InAs$_{y}$Sb$_{1-y}$ heterostructures as a promising alternative. Several of these predictions are supported by experimental observations, including quantized helical edge transport up to 60 K and the unconventional quantum Hall effect.   Defended on March 25, 2026, at the University of Montpellier. Jury: Michel GOIRAN (chair and rapporteur, LNCMI-CNRS, Toulouse); Alexey KAVOKIN (rapporteur, Westlake University, Hangzhou); Robson FERREIRA (rapporteur, LPENS-CNRS, Paris); Alexei BARANOV (member, IES-CNRS, Montpellier); Benoit JOUAULT and Frédéric TEPPE (members, L2C-CNRS, Montpellier).
summary: This comprehensive Habilitation thesis reviews the physics of pseudo-relativistic fermions and topological states in semiconductor heterostructures. It details how material parameters like temperature and strain can drive topological phase transitions, predicting novel quantum states like QSHIs and Dirac semimetals. The work bridges advanced theory with experimental observations in III-V semiconductor platforms.
main_problem: The research investigates the physics of pseudo-relativistic fermions and topological electronic states within zinc-blende semiconductor heterostructures.
main_result: The work predicts and discusses the existence of topological phases, such as Quantum Spin Hall Insulators and 2D Higher-Order Topological Insulators, in these low-dimensional semiconductor systems.
method: The approach combines theoretical modeling of band structures and many-body effects with the analysis of experimental measurements like magnetotransport and photoconductivity.
model_or_system: The primary systems are zinc-blende semiconductors and their heterostructures (e.g., HgCdTe, InAs/GaSb), studied in quantum wells and superlattices. The physics is governed by pseudo-relativistic fermion behavior.
key_observables: Quantized helical edge transport, Landau level collapse, Quantum Spin Hall Insulator signatures, and Dirac fermion behavior.
important_parameters: Temperature, applied pressure, electric fields, and magnetic fields are key tuning parameters for observing phase transitions.
main_assumptions: The work often relies on analyzing the interplay between single-particle band structure effects and electron-electron interaction effects.
figures_summary: Not specified, as the notes summarize the scope rather than describing specific figures.
paper_structure: The HDR memoir is structured thematically, progressing from bulk HgCdTe studies to phase transitions in HgTe QWs, and finally detailing the potential of III-V QW heterostructures for topological physics.
why_interesting: The strong focus on topological phases, Dirac fermions, and band inversion in solid-state systems provides rich material for understanding emergent quantum phenomena relevant to quantum materials research.
